from: FR-1 (mgmt-pg) — offered by the consumer that found it the hard way
appliesTo: every engine whose `tx` block is present
invariant: the audit row and the write that caused it commit or roll back together, or neither happened
why: A transaction belongs to the CONNECTION, not the pool. A transaction-local query issued on a pool handle runs autocommit while the rest of the transaction runs inside it. That surfaced in practice as a MISSING FOR UPDATE LOCK — not as leaked SQL — and was misread once before it was caught. A dialect-level suite is the only place this can be pinned once for every engine.
identity: Every step inserts ids EXPLICITLY, so this fixture is identity-agnostic and needs no `identity.autoAssigns`. Do not assume ids appear for free: `id {identity.ddl}` parses on Postgres and does NOT auto-assign (spec/02 Trap 2), so a porting language that omits ids will fail here for the wrong reason.
schema: CREATE TABLE item (id {identity.ddl}, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE audit (id {identity.ddl}, item_id INTEGER, note TEXT NOT NULL)

steps: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM item) AS items, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit) AS audits
assert: both rows are present after COMMIT
cases.why: the plain case the other two are measured against: one unit, two tables, COMMIT. If this fails the connection is not running the statements the fixture thinks it is.

steps: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM item) AS items, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit) AS audits
cases.why: the direction that catches a driver treating ROLLBACK as a no-op or as COMMIT: neither write may survive.

the injected failure must SURFACE, not be swallowed — a handler that discards store errors makes this test vacuous. The failing step is marked rather than the case, because the case continues: the point is what ROLLBACK leaves behind.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO audit (item_id, note) VALUES (1, NULL)

steps: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM item) AS items
assert: the NOT NULL violation is reported, and the item write is gone

steps: SELECT COUNT(*) AS items FROM item
assert: the outer write survives; the inner one does not
cases.why: savepoints are declared per engine; the case pins that a rollback to the savepoint discards only the inner write, leaving the outer one to COMMIT.

steps: SELECT id FROM item WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE
assert: the lock is taken within the transaction — a pool-handle statement here would run autocommit and take no lock
cases.why: a lock is taken only on the connection that owns the transaction — the failure txOwnership exists to make visible, and one that arrives as a missing lock rather than as an error.

assert: the level is accepted, or the engine declares no isolationLevels and the case is SKIPPED
cases.why: isolation is declared per engine, so a consumer may set it; an engine with no declared levels gates the case out rather than pretending.

runnerObligation: Run each case on a FRESH database. Assert the `requires` capability against contracts/engines.json FIRST: a case whose capability the engine does not declare is SKIPPED, never failed. A skip must be reported as a skip, because 'this engine cannot express it' and 'this engine failed it' are different facts and only one of them is a defect.
